hints: Think about what changes in the nucleus as atomic number increases across Period 3, while the outer electrons stay in the same shell.
Link the stronger pull on the outer electron to the energy needed to remove it, remembering that shielding stays approximately constant.
walkthrough:
Picture what first ionisation energy measures**
Think of it as how tightly the nucleus holds the outer electron. The reaction is $\text{X(g)} \rightarrow \text{X}^{+}\text{(g)} + \text{e}^{-}$. If the pull is stronger, you need more energy to pull the electron away.

Track protons versus shielding across the period**
Moving from $\text{Na}$ to $\text{Ar}$, each step adds one proton to the nucleus and one electron to the same third shell. The inner shells doing the shielding stay the same, so shielding is very similar. That means the extra proton is not cancelled out, effective nuclear charge rises and atomic radius decreases, so the outer electron is held more strongly and ionisation energy generally increases.

Final answer: Across Period 3 nuclear charge / proton number increases.
Electrons are removed from the same shell with similar shielding, so attraction of nucleus for outer electrons increases and more energy is needed to remove an electron.

hints: Recall where the two elements before Mg sit in Period 3 and what their general ionisation energies are compared to Mg.
Think why a Group 0 element with a full stable octet is very hard to ionise, while a Group 1 element with one outer s electron is very easy to ionise.
walkthrough:
Identify the missing elements**
The graph starts at $\text{Mg}$. The two vertical lines to the left are therefore $\text{Ne}$ (end of Period 2, Group 0) then $\text{Na}$ (start of Period 3, Group 1). You are continuing the atomic number axis backwards.

Place Ne very high and Na very low**
$\text{Ne}$ has the very stable $1\text{s}^{2}2\text{s}^{2}2\text{p}^{6}$ octet, a small atom with high effective nuclear charge, so its first ionisation energy is much higher than any Period 3 value shown. $\text{Na}$ has the arrangement $1\text{s}^{2}2\text{s}^{2}2\text{p}^{6}3\text{s}^{1}$, the new $3\text{s}$ electron is far from the nucleus and well shielded, so it is lost very easily and its cross goes clearly below all the others.

Final answer: Cross on first vertical line (Ne, Group 0) placed clearly higher than Mg, P and all other crosses shown.
Cross on second vertical line (Na, Group 1) placed lower than Mg, Al and all other crosses shown.

hints: Write the outer electron configurations of Mg as $3\text{s}^{2}$ and Al as $3\text{s}^{2}3\text{p}^{1}$ and ask which electron is removed more easily.
Compare distance and shielding of a 3p electron with a 3s electron to explain the Mg to Al drop.
Write the 3p configurations of P as $3\text{p}^{3}$ with three unpaired electrons and S as $3\text{p}^{4}$ with one pair.
Think what happens when two negatively charged electrons share the same orbital in S.
walkthrough:
Write out what electron is actually lost**
$\text{Mg}$ is $1\text{s}^{2}2\text{s}^{2}2\text{p}^{6}3\text{s}^{2}$, so you remove a $3\text{s}$ electron. $\text{Al}$ is $1\text{s}^{2}2\text{s}^{2}2\text{p}^{6}3\text{s}^{2}3\text{p}^{1}$, so you remove the single $3\text{p}$ electron. Do not just say shielding, name the subshells.

Explain why the 3p electron is easier to lose**
The $3\text{p}$ electron is slightly higher in energy, on average a little further from the nucleus and shielded by the $3\text{s}^{2}$ electrons as well as the inner shells. It feels less net attraction, so despite the higher nuclear charge of Al, less energy is needed and ionisation energy drops from Mg to Al.

Compare P and S in the p subshell**
$\text{P}$ is $[\text{Ne}]3\text{s}^{2}3\text{p}_{x}^{1}3\text{p}_{y}^{1}3\text{p}_{z}^{1}$, three unpaired electrons in separate orbitals. $\text{S}$ is $[\text{Ne}]3\text{s}^{2}3\text{p}^{4}$, so one $3\text{p}$ orbital now contains a pair: $3\text{p}_{x}^{2}3\text{p}_{y}^{1}3\text{p}_{z}^{1}$.

Use pair repulsion for the P to S drop**
In S the two electrons sharing one orbital repel each other. That repulsion outweighs the increase in nuclear charge, so one of the paired electrons is easier to remove and first ionisation energy falls slightly from P to S.

Final answer: Mg to Al: Al outer electron lost is in $3\text{p}$ subshell, Mg outer electron lost is in $3\text{s}$ subshell. $3\text{p}$ is higher in energy / further from nucleus / more shielded, so less energy needed to remove.
P to S: S has a paired electrons in a $3\text{p}$ orbital whereas P has singly occupied orbitals. Pair repulsion makes electron easier to remove, so IE falls.

hints: Use melting point 987 K and solubility to decide if L has giant ionic or simple molecular structure.
Recall what happens when aqueous $\text{Mg}^{2+}$ meets $\text{NaOH(aq)}$ and write the expected precipitate.
Identify the white solid formed from M as silicon dioxide and the acidic gas in the fumes.
walkthrough:
Decode L from its physical state**
A white crystalline solid melting at $987\text{ K}$ is far too high for weak intermolecular forces. That screams giant ionic lattice with strong ionic attractions needing lots of heat to break. Of the Period 3 chlorides, $\text{NaCl}$ and $\text{MgCl}_{2}$ fit, but the $\text{NaOH}$ test decides it.

Use the NaOH precipitate to confirm L**
L dissolves to give a roughly neutral solution containing $\text{Mg}^{2+}\text{(aq)}$, often written as $\text{Mg(H}_{2}\text{O)}_{6}^{2+}\text{(aq)}$. Adding $\text{NaOH(aq)}$ precipitates white $\text{Mg(OH)}_{2}$, which is insoluble. The equation is $$\text{MgCl}_{2} + 2\text{NaOH} \rightarrow \text{Mg(OH)}_{2} + 2\text{NaCl}$$ So L is $\text{MgCl}_{2}$.

Final answer: L is $\text{MgCl}_{2}$ / magnesium chloride. Giant ionic with strong attractions, hence high mp 987 K and white crystalline solid. Dissolves to give approximately neutral solution containing $\text{Mg}^{2+}\text{(aq)}$ / $\text{Mg(H}_{2}\text{O)}_{6}^{2+}\text{(aq)}$. With $\text{NaOH}$ gives white precipitate of $\text{Mg(OH)}_{2}$: $\text{MgCl}_{2} + 2\text{NaOH} \rightarrow \text{Mg(OH)}_{2} + 2\text{NaCl}$.

hints: Use melting point 987 K and solubility to decide if L has giant ionic or simple molecular structure.
Use low boiling point 331 K and liquid state to decide if M is ionic or simple covalent molecular.
Identify the white solid formed from M as silicon dioxide and the acidic gas in the fumes.
walkthrough:
Decode M from its volatility**
A liquid boiling at only $331\text{ K}$ must be simple molecular with weak London forces between molecules, not a giant lattice. That points to $\text{SiCl}_{4}$, $\text{PCl}_{5}$ or similar covalent chloride.

Use vigorous hydrolysis to confirm M**
M is hydrolysed rapidly by cold water to give a strongly acidic solution, a white solid and white fumes. This is classic $\text{SiCl}_{4}$ hydrolysis, made possible by the Si atom being able to accept water. The products are white solid (hydrated) silica, $\text{SiO}_{2}$, and $\text{HCl}$ which dissolves to give hydrochloric acid and escapes as white fumes in moist air: $$\text{SiCl}_{4} + 2\text{H}_{2}\text{O} \rightarrow \text{SiO}_{2} + 4\text{HCl}$$ So M is $\text{SiCl}_{4}$.

Final answer: M is $\text{SiCl}_{4}$ / silicon tetrachloride. Simple molecular / simple covalent, hence liquid with low bp 331 K. Hydrolysed rapidly by cold water: $\text{SiCl}_{4} + 2\text{H}_{2}\text{O} \rightarrow \text{SiO}_{2} + 4\text{HCl}$. White solid is (hydrated) $\text{SiO}_{2}$, strongly acidic solution / white fumes are $\text{HCl}$ / hydrochloric acid.
